tldr: Davies shows how he runs open-weight Qwen models on a four-box NVIDIA DGX Spark cluster for privacy-bound offices, with serving numbers, pitfalls and KV-cache loading instead of RAG.
summary: Davies builds private AI systems for banks, accountants, law firms and medical clients that will not send client data to US clouds. Privacy is the main driver, but he also cites reproducibility of decisions years later, hosted providers' lack of SLAs, and quality that drifts after releases. When Mac Studios became hard to buy he moved to NVIDIA DGX Sparks (GB10, 128 GB unified memory) running vLLM, which is slower than llama.cpp or MLX for one user but serves many at once. One box gave about 300 tokens/s aggregate: roughly 12 tokens/s each for 32 users, or 34 each when spread over four boxes.

His hardware rule is to pick a model that fits on one box and add boxes for throughput and availability, rather than splitting a big model across machines. He wired four Sparks into a ring over the high-speed interconnect, then stopped using it: it added about 20 W per box, and Wi-Fi 7 suffices for SSH and copying models. On top his team built layers: a plain URL endpoint with a proxy for Claude Code, box reservations so code reviews do not slow client demos, encrypted per-user chat history for debugging, and a browser and iPhone dashboard with remote shutdown.

He runs two Qwen variants on two boxes each. Qwen 3.6 35B at Q4 serves eight users at full 256k context, or 30-50 agents at 64k, at 60-100 tokens/s with 0.1-0.2 s to first token. A larger Qwen model, which he rates near mid-2026 frontier coding models, fits two full-context instances per Spark; its 'extra high' effort reasoned until it ran out of tokens and scored worse than 'medium'. Other lessons: vLLM memory utilization around 0.7 to avoid crashes, hard reboots to clear fragmentation that shrinks usable context, and care with clock governors. Spare memory runs Whisper or Parakeet and Chatterbox for live Spanish-English meeting translation.

For compliance he pins model hash, seed and inputs so a KYC decision can be reproduced later. Instead of RAG he prefills a document once, writes its KV cache to disk (2-5 GB for a book) and reloads it in about 250 ms, giving sub-second answers on a Mac and about one second on a Spark, for example on the 270-page SpaceX S-1. He said layered summary caches searched 58 million tokens of SWIFT ISO 20022 documentation in under five seconds. In Q&A he stressed the setup is for documents and code review, not code generation, and recommended Hermes Agent for home use.
keyPoints: One DGX Spark with vLLM produced about 300 tokens/s aggregate; 32 concurrent users got about 12 tokens/s each, and spreading them over four boxes raised that to about 34.
Choose a model that fits one box and scale by adding boxes; splitting a model across Sparks works but never doubles speed, and the interconnect cost about 20 W per box.
Qwen 3.6 35B at Q4 handled eight concurrent 256k-context sessions, or 30-50 at 64k, with 0.1-0.2 s time to first token.
On the larger Qwen model, the default 'extra high' effort performed worse than 'medium' because it exhausted its token budget while reasoning.
Operational settings: vLLM memory utilization around 0.7, hard reboots to undo memory fragmentation, and caution with CPU clock governors during benchmarks.
Saving a prefilled document's KV cache to disk and reloading it (about 250 ms for 2-5 GB) replaces chunking and embedding for stable documents.
Pinning model hash, seed and inputs makes regulated decisions such as KYC checks reproducible years later.
Davies said Spark prices were about to rise sharply and recommended buying soon.
takeaways: Benchmark candidate open-weight models on your own workload, not published leaderboards, before standardizing on one.
Pick a quantized model that fits a single machine and add identical machines for concurrency and failover.
Experiment with caching prefilled KV state to disk for large, rarely changing documents before building a RAG pipeline.
Record model hash, seed and inputs for any LLM-assisted decision you may need to justify later.
Give each user encrypted chat history and a reservation mechanism when sharing local inference boxes across an office.

quotes.text: You should really be finding the model that fits on these boxes. And if it doesn't fit on one box, it's questionable whether it's worth putting it on two boxes.
We use it for code reading, not for code writing.

watchIf: You need LLMs for a regulated or privacy-sensitive organization and want concrete numbers and pitfalls from running open-weight models on a small on-premises cluster.
